<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/hyper-na-euv-the-next-extension-beyond-high-na-lithography-carl-zeiss-asml/">Hyper-NA EUV: The Next Extension Beyond High NA Lithography (Carl Zeiss, ASML)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>Carl Zeiss SMT</strong> and <strong>ASML</strong> published a technical paper titled “Hyper-NA: a system with a numerical aperture of at least 0.75.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Summary:</strong></p>
<p>The researchers examine Hyper-NA EUV lithography with a numerical aperture of at least 0.75 as a path beyond current 0.55-NA High-NA systems, including the optical architecture, resolution potential, reticle 3D effects, polarization, and requirements for extending the existing EUV ecosystem.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.spiedigitallibrary.org/journals/journal-of-micro-nanopatterning-materials-and-metrology/volume-25/issue-4/041807/Hyper-NA-a-system-with-a-numerical-aperture-of-at-least-0-75/10.1117%2F1.JMM.25.4.041807.full">Find the technical paper here</a>. October 2026.</p>
<p>Patra, Michael, Heiko Feldmann, Jens Timo Neumann, and Gerardo Bottiglieri. “Hyper-NA: a system with a numerical aperture of at least 0.75.” Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials, and Metrology 25, no. 4 (2026): 041807. https://doi.org/10.1117/1.JMM.25.4.041807</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>

		<title>Thermal Complexity Grows With AI Chips And Photonics</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/thermal-complexity-grows-with-ai-chips-and-photonics/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/thermal-complexity-grows-with-ai-chips-and-photonics/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Ed Sperling]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 07 Oct 2026 07:01:34 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Low Power-High Performance]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Round Tables]]></category>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Increasing power density makes heat, stress, and aging harder to predict, and more critical to address earlier in the design flow.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/thermal-complexity-grows-with-ai-chips-and-photonics/">Thermal Complexity Grows With AI Chips And Photonics</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Photonics can speed up the movement of data using less energy, but the impact of heat, warpage, and other stresses needs to be fully understood up front.</li>
<li>Understanding the transient behavior associated with multi-die assemblies is complex, but it opens the door to much more granular performance and thermal optimization.</li>
<li>Tools that can accurately predict thermally accelerated aging are lacking today.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p><strong>Experts at the Table: </strong>Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss the impact of heat on photonics, transient behavior, and system reliability, with Lang Lin, director of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/silvaco-inc/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/silvaco-inc/">Silvaco</a>; Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/vinci/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/vinci/">Vinci</a>; Chris Mueth, director of new markets management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/keysight-technologies/">Keysight EDA</a>; and John Ferguson, senior director of product management at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/" data-uw-rm-brl="PR" data-uw-original-href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/mentor-a-siemens-business/">Siemens EDA</a>. What follows are excerpts of that conversation, which was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. This is the second of a three-part series. Part one is <a href="https://semiengineering.com/scaling-thermal-analysis-from-transistors-to-data-centers/">here</a>.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24281366" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-12-at-3.00.47-PM.png?resize=1704%2C354&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1704" height="354" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-12-at-3.00.47-PM.png?w=1704&amp;ssl=1 1704w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-12-at-3.00.47-PM.png?resize=300%2C62&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-12-at-3.00.47-PM.png?resize=1024%2C213&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-12-at-3.00.47-PM.png?resize=768%2C160&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-12-at-3.00.47-PM.png?resize=1536%2C319&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-12-at-3.00.47-PM.png?resize=600%2C125&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>L-R: Silvaco&#8217;s Berg; Synopsys&#8217; Lin; Vinci&#8217;s Radhakrishnan; Keysight&#8217;s Mueth; Siemens&#8217; Ferguson.</strong></p>
<p><strong>SE: Moving data takes power, which generates heat. So how do we keep data moving while still remaining within the power budget? Is the solution photonics? Even there, heat can cause issues.</strong></p>
<p><strong>Mueth</strong>: Photonics has a lot of promise for reducing data center bottlenecks, but it can&#8217;t be scaled right now. Building a large mesh switch requires many components, and you have high losses. So you have to revisit the whole architecture for how things are done in photonics and do them differently, probably in a modular style that&#8217;s scalable. Another issue is heat sensitivity. You have to stabilize that. But even then, your photonic structure is going to have heaters in it because these have to be controlled. And if you have a large mesh switch, the amount of control you need is significant. So how do you calibrate your structures through that chip to get enough performance when you may have thousands of heaters that you have to control? If we can solve that problem, it will open things up a bit. But that still doesn&#8217;t get rid of the losses in the |photonics chips. That has to be solved with a modular, scalable architecture.</p>
<p><strong>SE: This leads to another issue, which is that you&#8217;re no longer dealing with just one type of processing element. What happens when you go from a GPU to a CPU? Do they both generate the same amount of heat? And is that, in turn, different when you have a high-intensity workload that&#8217;s short-lived? How do you cool everything down to keep temperatures consistent?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Radhakrishnan</strong>: Co-packaged optics is trying to solve that problem, to some extent, bringing the silicon photonics into the package, keeping it small for EICs/PICs. They are trying to thermally isolate it. But if you try to simulate the whole thing, the part that will be missing is the transient nature, and that&#8217;s what&#8217;s really needed. If you try to keep something far off, then the heat is going to take more time to get there, and by the time the next wave comes on an ASIC, the heat will still be there. Even a very small change in temperature can shift the ring oscillator. What&#8217;s needed is the ability to simulate the whole thing together in a transient domain to make sure it&#8217;s going to function reliably and optically. Being able to simulate one part of a system in a transient domain is key to making sure co-packaged optics is viable and that we can push it forward.</p>
<p><strong>Mueth</strong>: That&#8217;s a good point. The difference in time constants really messes things up. And if you&#8217;re doing co-packaged optics, the EIC driver typically would be mounted near or on top of your PIC, so you have heat pollution, which steers your photonics. You&#8217;re introducing new stresses, and those stresses have a very big impact on the optical signals — maybe bigger than thermal. You have to know what those trade-offs are, and make sure you&#8217;re taking them into consideration so that you&#8217;re combining the best of both. Just by moving something, you can make things worse instead of better.</p>
<p><strong>SE: And how do you know your thermal sensors are functioning properly all the time?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Mueth</strong>: You can do that in the calibration process. You can put a sniffing loop inside the photonic PIC, but it makes that incredibly complicated.</p>
<p><strong>Ferguson</strong>: We can try to move things to reduce some of the thermal that&#8217;s built up. But when you&#8217;re moving big elements, particularly like what we have in photonics, you&#8217;re introducing new stresses. Those have a very big impact on optical signals — maybe bigger than the thermal. So you have to know what those trade-offs are and make sure you&#8217;re taking them into consideration so that you&#8217;re combining the best of both.</p>
<p><strong>Lin</strong>: For silicon photonics, you can think about it as a type of analog circuit. When we deal with analog versus digital, the thermal behavior is very different. Digital transistors involve switching current. The current will supply the transistor&#8217;s on and off, so the Joule heating effect is not that bad. But for silicon photonics and analog devices, the DC current is always there, and there&#8217;s a big swing of signals. That creates current flowing through the interconnects, like a waveguide. It generates a lot of heat, and we need this heat for the CPO to work. That heat is needed to operate the EIC. But what if there are so many heaters together? How do you place them far enough away so that everything can operate, but not create hot spots within the heater area? Stress is another problem that has to be considered for silicon photonics to operate well.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Heat can cause warpage. If you put two warped chips together and they&#8217;re very thin, you may be able to flatten them, but at the same time you&#8217;ve probably lost some ability to dissipate heat due to thinner dies, right?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Berg</strong>: Thermal variation on a PIC chip generally results in a mismatch of features — much more so than in EIC circuits. If you&#8217;re talking about multi-physics and digital twins and surrogate models affiliated with EICs, you essentially can triple that need in photonics ICs because they&#8217;re much more sensitive to warpage and thermal gradients. A laser is a heat source that potentially creates a reliability problem. To that end, photonics needs a thermal understanding and a multi-physics confirmation of not only the electrical, mechanical, and thermal, but optical as well. So now you&#8217;ve got four solvers that you potentially have to do. It&#8217;s a bit more complicated than the electronics, and that&#8217;s the reason why photonics has been the next big thing in the semiconductor world for the past 30 years. It&#8217;s much more complicated from a physics perspective than anybody thought it would be.</p>
<p><strong>Mueth</strong>: Traditionally we were worried about thermal in semiconductors. We ignored the passives. Now, with photonics, you have thermal effects on the passives.</p>
<p><strong>SE: Within a chip you may have multiple dies, because you cannot get the performance you need out of a single die, especially in AI data centers. How do we coordinate the different dies within a package so you aren&#8217;t just running everything flat-out all the time?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Berg</strong>: You need to be very careful.</p>
<p><strong>SE: This is a complex orchestration problem, right? And it needs to be hierarchical.</strong></p>
<p><strong>Mueth</strong>: Yes, and when you&#8217;re doing the architecture, you&#8217;re going to have to model your thermals. One of the corners would be, &#8216;What are your high-performance use cases?&#8217; You have to model those thermally, electrically, and mechanically, so when you are farther down the design path you have a higher chance of success. But that modeling has to be done up front.</p>
<p><strong>Ferguson</strong>: You can do each of those standalone variables, but then you&#8217;re not getting the full story. You have to do them all consecutively, which means that what you&#8217;re doing is running each one many, many times, one after another, until you get to a steady state. And then you hope that is the correct steady state. That depends on what you&#8217;re building.</p>
<p><strong>Radhakrishnan</strong>: If you look at the direction AI chips are going, they&#8217;re trying to get from training to inference. They are trying to increase the bandwidth. That&#8217;s what is driving all the chips to be stacked on top of each other, and that affects their behavior. They want to understand the inference behavior. But it&#8217;s not just about peak performance. How much higher is the temperature going to be in transient? If I have much more headroom, because it&#8217;s only going to last for a nanosecond, maybe I can go to extra power. But is that nanosecond going to come every millisecond or microsecond? How often am I going to allow peak power? And how much of the thermal budget can I push and let the data center people create a design rule that says, &#8216;For inference, I can allow a millisecond pulse every 100 milliseconds.&#8217; This is a huge new paradigm that people can exploit when they go to different use cases. It&#8217;s all driven by what the end user wants and how they want to achieve the maximum performance they need.</p>
<p><strong>Lin</strong>: Going back to the question about hierarchical models, those are important not only to deal with the capacity to simulate thermal for an AI chip, but also to enable an ecosystem with different vendors providing their model hierarchically. For example, HBM vendors have to provide some kind of model for an HBM chip. Then they send that to a system integration house, which will combine different models, build a whole multi-die stack, and run thermal. First, they need to consider the impact of the vendor&#8217;s model on thermal. Second, they need to finalize the whole system. They&#8217;re the final product delivery hub. They have to make sure all the models are connected, assembled, and then simulate the whole system. So the hierarchical model is a must, and not only for capacity. The industry is working on this. We need the ecosystem to deliver a model, and we have to agree on standards so that everybody can share their models and the integrators can assemble them.</p>
<p><strong>SE: One of the big concerns in data centers is aging of data paths due to electromigration, which is accelerated by heat. How does that impact the overall design process?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Radhakrishnan</strong>: I&#8217;m seeing a lot of thermal sensors being embedded into the die for aging. Those have to be on-chip to determine degradation over time. Then, you can throttle parts of the chip. But everything is packaged up, so it has to be done by software getting some sensing information back, and then you see what changes you can make. This is even more of an issue with automotive, where chips have to last 10 to 15 years. That&#8217;s where you need to do simulation to determine if you&#8217;re putting the sensors in the right location. Can I get the right sensing back so a chip can function over time as things change? You need to be able to capture all that, and this is the direction companies are heading.</p>
<p><strong>SE: This can vary by ambient temperature, right?</strong></p>
<p><strong>Berg</strong>: Yes, particularly places like Saudi Arabia. The simple rule of thumb is the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrhenius_equation">Arrhenius equation</a>. Every 10 degrees results in a substantial reduction in reliability. This is really important to get right.</p>
<p><strong>Lin</strong>: But I don&#8217;t see a lot of tools in the industry for accurately predicting thermally induced aging. There&#8217;s a gap. We need tools to pair the correct equation so we can predict aging effects, and how to resolve them. Sensors are a way to monitor the aging effects, but what&#8217;s happening on the design optimization side? No one has done that for aging-aware design optimization.</p>
<p><strong>Radhakrishnan</strong>: It&#8217;s an under-design/over-design kind of problem. That&#8217;s why, ideally, it has to be dynamic over time. And that is a huge problem.</p>
<hr />

Rising power density and chiplet complexity drive thermal considerations earlier in the design process.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>CFETs and buried power rails; agentic AI for EDA; 6G architecture decisions; chiplet connectivity.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/blog-review-oct-7-3/">Blog Review: Oct. 7</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Siemens’ Karen Chow, Sheetal Veronica, and Kunjesh Agashiwala explore how <a href="https://blogs.sw.siemens.com/calibre/2026/09/30/solving-the-extraction-challenges-of-cfet-and-backside-power/">CFETs and buried power rails</a> come together to reduce the chip area needed, improve power efficiency, and help meet the high-performance needs of AI accelerators, data centers and mobile processors.</p>
<p>Synopsys’ Thomas Andersen says the strongest results come when <a href="https://www.synopsys.com/blogs/chip-design/agentic-ai-design-knowledge.html">agentic AI</a> can leverage the company-specific knowledge that makes each engineering organization distinct, such as its methodologies, design history, priorities, best practices, and accumulated experience.</p>
<p>Cadence’s Reela Samuel considers what separates agentic AI from traditional and AI-assisted <a href="https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/artificial-intelligence/posts/what-agentic-ai-actually-does-in-eda">EDA workflows</a>, noting that while individual operations in the loop are not necessarily new, what changes is how those operations can be coordinated.</p>
<p>Keysight’s Stephen Douglas urges the industry to start rapid prototyping of the hardest <a href="https://www.keysight.com/blogs/en/tech/automation-and-assurance/evolving-to-the-ai-native-core">6G architectural questions</a> as the window narrows to turn promising concepts into mature standards, interoperable products, and deployable systems.</p>
<p>Arm’s Francisco Socal introduces <a href="https://developer.arm.com/community/arm-community-blogs/b/soc-design-and-simulation-blog/posts/amba-c2c-moving-forward-with-a-converged-amba-foundation-for-c2c-connectivity">AMBA C2C</a>, which extends chiplet connectivity across AXI and CHI with scalable protocol subsets, interoperability, and flexible transport support for fully coherent, advanced heterogeneous compute.</p>
<p>SEMI’s Saifi Usmani highlights finalists in the <a href="https://www.semi.org/en/blogs/finalists-for-semi-startups-for-sustainable-semiconductors-to-present-live-pitches-at-semicon-west-2026">Startups for Sustainable Semiconductors</a> program, which offer solutions from monolithic integrated voltage regulators to wafer defect inspection and characterization to a GPU-native physics simulation platform.</p>
<p>Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest <a href="https://semiengineering.com/newsletter/auto-security-and-ai-oct-2026/">Automotive, Security &amp; AI newsletter</a>:</p>
<p>Infineon’s Karthik Rangarajan shows how <a href="https://semiengineering.com/memory-at-the-edge-non-volatile-memory-challenges-and-requirements-for-humanoid-robots/">distributed NVM</a> supports high-endurance telemetry logging, functional safety, and time-sensitive networking where resilience is critical.</p>
<p>Rambus’ Vincent van der Leest demonstrates how <a href="https://semiengineering.com/open-security-foundations-are-only-the-beginning-deploying-caliptra-hardware-in-production/">roots of trust</a> are beginning to assume a broader role as platform security orchestrators.</p>
<p>Cadence’s Kartik Hegde looks <a href="https://semiengineering.com/why-llms-are-the-best-thing-to-happen-to-chip-design/">beyond RTL</a> to a new representation that allows engineers to express intent more intuitively.</p>
<p>Synopsys’ Brian Davenport outlines a development flow to ensure that hardware can do its job in the field without being vulnerable to <a href="https://semiengineering.com/mitigating-threats-with-pre-silicon-security-verification/">attacks or leakage</a> of private data.</p>
<p>Siemens EDA’s Kartik Sahajpal and Prashant Dixit dig into integration and verification challenges in <a href="https://semiengineering.com/crossing-chiplet-boundaries-with-pcie-over-ucie/">PCIe-over-UCIe</a> systems, including how link-state transitions affect transaction behavior.</p>
<p>Imagination’s Alex Pim examines <a href="https://semiengineering.com/llm-performance-and-acceleration-part-1/">time to first token</a> and inter-token latency, and how they apply to the two main stages of LLM compute — prefill and decode.</p>
<p>Keysight’s Marc Witteman contends that compliance with <a href="https://semiengineering.com/us-executive-order-on-energy-grid-supply-chain-security/">trade restrictions</a> is no longer about proving where a device was built, but about how the product works.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/blog-review-oct-7-3/">Blog Review: Oct. 7</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>Seoul National University</strong> and <strong>Yonsei University</strong> published a technical paper titled “Monolithic three-dimensionally integrated memristor-thin-film transistor for electrically programmable multimode reservoir computing.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“Reservoir computing offers an efficient framework for processing temporal information, but most hardware reservoirs exhibit fixed or narrowly tunable dynamics determined by intrinsic material relaxation time. A monolithically integrated memristor-thin-film transistor reservoir kernel of this study enables electrically programmable temporal dynamics across a wide timescale. By vertically and monolithically integrating Ru/HfO<sub>2</sub>/TiN memristors with In<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> channel thin-film transistors (TFTs), the memristive conductance dynamics are modulated by the TFTs.”</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-78364-5">technical paper here</a>. October 2026.</p>
<p>Shim, Sung Keun, Wonho Choi, Sunwoo Cheong, Dong Hoon Shin, Jonghoon Shin, Janguk Han, Jiseong Im, et al. “Monolithic three-dimensionally integrated memristor-thin-film transistor for electrically programmable multimode reservoir computing.” Nature Communications (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78364-5</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at ETH Zürich, CISPA, and New York University published a technical paper titled “Terracotta: Enabling the Adoption of New DRAM Techniques via a Flexible DRAM Interface and Memory Controller.” Abstract Excerpt: “DRAM continues to limit the performance, energy efficiency, and robustness of modern systems. Many prior works propose DRAM techniques that support in-DRAM computation,... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/programmable-memory-controller-eases-adoption-of-new-dram-techniques-eth-zurich-cispa-nyu/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/programmable-memory-controller-eases-adoption-of-new-dram-techniques-eth-zurich-cispa-nyu/">Programmable Memory Controller Eases Adoption of New DRAM Techniques (ETH Zürich, CISPA, NYU)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>ETH Zürich, CISPA</strong>, and <strong>New York University</strong> published a technical paper titled “Terracotta: Enabling the Adoption of New DRAM Techniques via a Flexible DRAM Interface and Memory Controller.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“DRAM continues to limit the performance, energy efficiency, and robustness of modern systems. Many prior works propose DRAM techniques that support in-DRAM computation, improve memory access latency and parallelism, and enhance DRAM maintenance and reliability. However, adopting each new technique requires repeated modifications to the rigid DRAM interface and memory controller, hindering its deployment. Our goal is to reduce these repeated modifications. We observe that the DRAM commands and memory controller structures of many DRAM techniques are similar. Our key idea is to use these similarities to compose a set of primitives for implementing diverse DRAM techniques. We propose Terracotta, a new framework with two flexible components: (i) custom command extensions that let DRAM vendors define new commands within a single, standardized interface, and (ii) a programmable memory controller that system designers can program to support new DRAM techniques post-silicon. Together, these enable deployment by configuring the memory controller instead of modifying the interface and controller. ”</p>
<p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06475">Find the technical paper here</a>. October 2026.</p>
<p>Songara, Harsh, Konstantinos Kanellopoulos, F. Nisa Bostancı, Konstantinos Marios Sgouras, Ataberk Olgun, İsmail Emir Yüksel, Andreas Kosmas Kakolyris, A. Giray Yağlıkçı, and Onur Mutlu. “Terracotta: Enabling the Adoption of New DRAM Techniques via a Flexible DRAM Interface and Memory Controller.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.06475 (October 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.06475</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>

		<title>Advancing The CFET-Based Device Roadmap: Novel Integration Modules And Standard Cell Configurations</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/advancing-the-cfet-based-device-roadmap-novel-integration-modules-and-standard-cell-configurations-2/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/advancing-the-cfet-based-device-roadmap-novel-integration-modules-and-standard-cell-configurations-2/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Geert Hellings]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 06 Oct 2026 07:01:13 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Perspectives & Analysis]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[The Imec Report]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[CFETs]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[complementary FET]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[design-technology co-optimization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[DTCO]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[imec]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[NanoIC Pilot Line]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[routability]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[SRAM]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[standard cells]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[transistors]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24282399</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Part 2: Toward scalable sCFET standard cell architectures: split-gate devices, a 5T+1 CFET SRAM bit cell, and improved back-end-of-line routability.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/advancing-the-cfet-based-device-roadmap-novel-integration-modules-and-standard-cell-configurations-2/">Advancing The CFET-Based Device Roadmap: Novel Integration Modules And Standard Cell Configurations</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>From the A7 logic technology node onwards, industry may likely transition to CFET-based transistor architectures which enable 4.5-track (4.5T) and below standard cells.</li>
<li>Progress in CFET enablement is backed by two complementary R&amp;D tracks, with imec pioneering many of the underlying innovations: the development of CFET-specific process modules, and a design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) exploration of scalable standard cell configurations.</li>
<li>Part 1 of this two-part article presents two optimized CFET-specific modules: (1) a backside contact module; and (2) a gate-stack integration module that enables multiple threshold voltages in nanosheet and CFET devices.</li>
<li>Part 2 covers imec’s latest CFET DTCO studies. A novel scalable architecture for sequential CFET is presented that enables split-gate and common-gate device options, key in advancing both the logic and SRAM scaling roadmaps. Another DTCO study presents improved routability at the back-end-of-line (BEOL) level to support the scaling of CFET standard cells.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<h2>CFET technology moving forward, backed by integration efforts and DTCO studies</h2>
<p>The semiconductor industry is going through a major architectural transition, with gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors replacing FinFETs in advanced logic nodes of 3nm and beyond. GAA nanosheet transistor technology offers scalability down to the A10 logic generation, where it enables 5.5-track (T) standard cells – the track being a measure for the standard cell height.</p>
<p>For the A7 node, options are becoming increasingly diverse to meet the growing diversification of application needs, driven by the AI revolution. According to imec’s latest roadmap, one option is to design systems around imec’s CMOS 2.0 scaling paradigm. With CMOS 2.0, a system-on-chip (SoC) is partitioned into heterogeneous, functional tiers each optimized using the most suitable technology, and reconnected using 3D interconnect technologies. For other use cases, GAA nanosheet technology may be pushed to its ultimate scaling limits, with power delivered from either the frontside or the backside. But industry may as well transition to complementary FET (CFET) device architectures. By stacking p and nMOS transistors on top of each other, standard cells can be further scaled down to 3T, thereby extending the classical CMOS logic roadmap to at least the A3 technology node.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282400" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig1-roadmap.webp?resize=1798%2C1012&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1798" height="1012" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig1-roadmap.webp?w=1798&amp;ssl=1 1798w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig1-roadmap.webp?resize=300%2C169&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig1-roadmap.webp?resize=1024%2C576&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig1-roadmap.webp?resize=768%2C432&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig1-roadmap.webp?resize=1536%2C865&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig1-roadmap.webp?resize=600%2C338&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Imec’s logic technology roadmap.</strong></p>
<p>Imec and its industrial partners are working to make CFET-based devices manufacturable. In recent years, they laid the groundwork for key integration approaches, categorized as monolithic CFET (mCFET) and sequential CFET (sCFET) [1,2].</p>
<p>Both approaches start from the vertical stacking of Si/SiGe layers from which the n and pFETs are fabricated. With mCFET, the vertical device structure with common top and bottom gates is patterned and processed in a single sequence of process steps. The patterning, deposition and selective removal of materials around and in between the high-aspect ratio device structure requires considerable effort in terms of module development. sCFET, on the contrary, patterns the top and bottom devices independently using dedicated masks. With sCFET, the individual process steps are simpler compared to mCFET but some critical steps need to be executed twice – for top and bottom separately. sCFET additionally involves two wafer flips, distorting the wafer and challenging the precise alignment of front-to-back device connections. Pending further progress in alignment accuracy, mCFET is believed to offer the fastest path to industrial adoption.</p>
<p>Progress in CFET integration is complemented with design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) studies that examine CFET device architectures from a circuit level perspective [2]. These studies aim to identify scalable standard cell configurations and performance boosters that offer the best tradeoff in terms of power, performance, area and cost.</p>
<p>In this 2-part article, we report major progress in CFET device integration, and we discuss CFET scalability using DTCO studies.</p>
<p>In part 1 [link], two process modules were presented that are essential for both mCFET and sCFET device flavors: (1) a backside contact module, and (2) a gate stack integration approach that enables multiple threshold voltages (V<sub>t</sub>) in nanosheet and CFET devices.</p>
<p>In part 2, a scalable architecture for sCFET is introduced, allowing both split-gate and common-gate configurations. Besides progressing the logic roadmap, DTCO work shows how this split-gate architecture also benefits CFET-based SRAM scaling. Finally, improved back-end-of-line (BEOL) routability is demonstrated, supporting the scaling of CFET standard cells.</p>
<p>The reported results are achieved in the framework of the imec-hosted European NanoIC pilot line, which is targeting the development of beyond-2nm systems-on-chip. CFET development, which is centered on CFET-specific designs, process steps, modules and baseline flows, has been selected as one of the key enabling technologies for extending the logic roadmap into the ångström era. This will help Europe to remain at the forefront of next-generation semiconductor innovation and manufacturing.</p>
<h2>A novel architecture for sCFET: Split-gate device architecture enlarges CFET’s scaling potential</h2>
<p>Earlier DTCO studies have already demonstrated the scaling potential of CFET technology across subsequent logic nodes – a prerequisite for the semiconductor industry to adopt the new device architecture. For mCFET, for example, imec previously identified the double-row (DR) CFET architecture as the most optimal way to integrate mCFETs into an A7 standard cell [3]. A double-row CFET standard cell contains two rows of stacked devices with a shared vertical signal via in between, and power walls at the cell boundary (see Figure 2). Later, layout inefficiencies were addressed, resulting in an optimized version of the double-row CFET: the half-height double-row (hDR) architecture. At IEDM 2025, additional scaling boosters such as the integration of hybrid channels were introduced to support aggressive area scaling targets towards A3 [2].</p>
<h3>Common-gate and split-gate devices: The challenge of offering both flavors with one device architecture</h3>
<p>The process flow for fabricating mCFET devices inherently offers common-gate devices: the gates of n and pFETs are structurally connected to one another. This works well for 90-95% of all basic logic gates – think about an inverter circuit (or NOT gate) that performs the logical operation of negation. But for other logic circuits, such as flipflops and multiplex gates, independent control of n and pFET metal gates is desired. One way to address this need is to leave one polarity of the stacked CFET device unused (for example, only using the nFETs, and removing the pFETs). While this approach solves the gate control issue, it does not fully exploit the area benefit of stacking n and pFETs.</p>
<p>sCFET device architectures, where top and bottom devices are patterned independently, can offer split-gate devices in a more natural way. But conventional sCFET architectures leave us with the opposite problem: an extra module is needed to connect the gates for those circuits that need it.</p>
<h3>A double-flip sCFET architecture: Offering both options in an area efficient way</h3>
<p>At 2026 VLSI, imec introduces the double-flip sCFET architecture that offers both split-gate and common-gate device options without compromising area efficiency [4].</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282401" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig2-CFET-architectures.webp?resize=1401%2C691&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1401" height="691" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig2-CFET-architectures.webp?w=1401&amp;ssl=1 1401w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig2-CFET-architectures.webp?resize=300%2C148&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig2-CFET-architectures.webp?resize=1024%2C505&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig2-CFET-architectures.webp?resize=768%2C379&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig2-CFET-architectures.webp?resize=600%2C296&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 2: Cross-sectional views of (a) double-row mCFET (DR), (b) half-height double-row (hDR) with dense backside metal-0 tracks (BM0), (c) hDR with split gate, and (d) sCFET with split-gate and dense BM0 </strong><strong>(as presented at 2026 VLSI)</strong><strong>. (CH = standard cell height; NSH = nanosheet channels; MRW = shared signal wall; VMM = via that can bypass the bottom device; MD = metal-to-diffusion layer)</strong></p>
<p>The impact of the new architecture in terms of area efficiency and routability was evaluated for various CFET-based libraries, designed around, for example, AND, OR and inverter circuits. With an overall library efficiency (h) as high as 98%, the new sCFET double-flip architecture provides the most efficient area utilization compared to double-row (DR) and half-height double-row (hDR) mCFET architectures. When combined with dense backside metal-0 (BM0) routing, the new architecture supports 3T standard cells that will be needed in A3 and A2 logic nodes – according to imec’s latest technology roadmap.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282403" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig3-Cell-area.webp?resize=1438%2C753&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1438" height="753" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig3-Cell-area.webp?w=1438&amp;ssl=1 1438w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig3-Cell-area.webp?resize=300%2C157&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig3-Cell-area.webp?resize=1024%2C536&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig3-Cell-area.webp?resize=768%2C402&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig3-Cell-area.webp?resize=600%2C314&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 3: Cell area breakdown of CFET libraries, for each of the CFET architectures (double row (DR), half-height double-row (hDR), hDR with dense backside metal-0 routing (hDR/dense BMO), and double-flip sCFET). sCFET significantly optimizes cell library and achieves an overall 98% layout efficiency (</strong><strong>h</strong><strong><sub>layout</sub></strong><strong>) </strong><strong>(as presented at 2026 VLSI)</strong><strong>.</strong></p>
<p>The double-flip sCFET flow starts from a bonded stack with an embedded middle dielectric isolation (eMDI) between top and bottom devices [2]. First, the top device is patterned from the frontside, and the top gate is finished partly during the replacement metal-gate module. After wafer flip and wafer thinning, the bottom device is patterned from the backside. Next, a via connection between bottom and top gate is optionally provided, which can be utilized for common-gate use cases. Following a second wafer flip, processing of the top and bottom devices is completed.</p>
<p>Additional scaling potential is offered by the possibility to introduce hybrid channels, optimized for n and pFETs separately. Think about CFET devices with different channel orientations for the top and bottom devices, or CFETs with asymmetric sheet widths. This brings along extra power-performance-area benefits and supports design flexibility.</p>
<h2>A 5T+1 CFET SRAM bit cell: Split-gate sCFET device architecture prolongs the SRAM scaling roadmap</h2>
<p>Static random-access memory (SRAM) continues to be industry’s main workhorse for providing on-chip cache memory – the high-speed memory that interfaces between dynamic RAM (DRAM) and XPU. A conventional SRAM memory bit cell consists of six transistors: four nFETs and two pFETs (or, alternatively, two nFETs and four pFETs). Of these FETs, two nFETs and two pFETs (PUx and PDx in Figures 5 and 6) are paired to form two cross-coupled inverters, able to store one bit of information. The remaining nFETs are designed as pass-gate transistors (PGs), connecting to the bit and word lines (BL, WL) and controlling the data flow during the read and write operations.</p>
<h3>The SRAM density crisis: Can CFET bring relief?</h3>
<p>Just as in logic technology, the density increase of SRAM memory relies on dimensional scaling of the bit cells, in combination with device architecture innovations. But since the 7nm technology node, SRAM bit cell scaling has fallen flat compared to logic CMOS device scaling. This asymmetry in scaling potential presents considerable challenges for chip designers. Even the transition to GAA-nanosheet-based 6T SRAM cells could not provide the required power, performance, and area benefits. CFET-based 6T SRAM technology is expected to bring initial relief, as the stacking of (part of) the n and pFETs (i.e., PUx and PDx) can substantially increase the SRAM bit cell density.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282405" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig4-SRAM-density-crisis.webp?resize=1920%2C1242&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1920" height="1242" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig4-SRAM-density-crisis.webp?w=1920&amp;ssl=1 1920w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig4-SRAM-density-crisis.webp?resize=300%2C194&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig4-SRAM-density-crisis.webp?resize=1024%2C662&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig4-SRAM-density-crisis.webp?resize=768%2C497&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig4-SRAM-density-crisis.webp?resize=1536%2C994&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig4-SRAM-density-crisis.webp?resize=600%2C388&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 4: The SRAM density crisis. The blue symbols represent imec’s options for high-density SRAMs, including single row, double-row, optimized double-row, and the new 5T+1 architecture </strong><strong>(as presented at 2026 VLSI)</strong><strong>. </strong></p>
<p>But even in the CFET SRAM era, further area reduction is being challenged, as the 6T SRAM bit cell does not map efficiently onto a CFET-based architecture. While the two inverters can be mapped using a stacked n/p device architecture (PUx and PDx), the two nFETs serving as the single pass-gate transistors (PGs) leave the two top p-type transistors of the CFET device stack unused. As a result, the intrinsic vertical density advantage of CFET cannot fully translate into bit cell area scaling for a 6T SRAM. A 5T SRAM bit cell configuration with only one single pass-gate transistor has been investigated as an area-efficient alternative, but writability and noise issues have challenged its adoption.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282406" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig5-6T-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=1407%2C830&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1407" height="830" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig5-6T-CFET-SRAM.webp?w=1407&amp;ssl=1 1407w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig5-6T-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=300%2C177&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig5-6T-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=1024%2C604&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig5-6T-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=768%2C453&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig5-6T-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=600%2C354&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 5: Schematic representation of a conventional 6T SRAM, which does not map nicely onto a CFET </strong><strong>(as presented at 2026 VLSI)</strong><strong>. (WL = word lines; BL and BLB = bit lines; PUx and PDx form the cross-coupled invertors storing 1 bit of information; VSS and VDD are power supply lines)</strong></p>
<h3>A promising 5T+1 SRAM CFET architecture: Enabled by sCFET split-gate devices</h3>
<p>Imec’s novel sCFET architecture for split-gate devices now opens doors to continued SRAM density scaling – as presented at 2026 VLSI [5]. In a novel 5T+1 architecture, the two single pass-gate transistors (PGs) are replaced with one CFET transmission-gate device (TG) that pairs an nFET and a pFET. Such a transmission gate needs independent n and p gate control, which can be enabled by implementing imec’s novel sCFET split-gate device. As such, a 5T-like SRAM bit cell (i.e., a single-ended SRAM bit cell with sCFET transmission gate) can be realized while maintaining a 5T footprint. The use of the transmission gate as the access device also improves writability compared to a ‘classic’ 5T implementation.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282407" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig6-5T-1-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=1080%2C807&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1080" height="807" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig6-5T-1-CFET-SRAM.webp?w=1080&amp;ssl=1 1080w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig6-5T-1-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=300%2C224&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig6-5T-1-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=1024%2C765&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig6-5T-1-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=768%2C574&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig6-5T-1-CFET-SRAM.webp?resize=600%2C448&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 6: Schematic representation of a 5T+1 CFET SRAM with transmission gate </strong><strong>(as presented at 2026 VLSI)</strong><strong>. (BL = bit line; WLn and WLp are word lines connecting to the n and p FETs of the transmission gate (TG); VSS and VDD are power supply lines)</strong></p>
<p>SRAM operation can be further improved by optimizing layout and routability at the memory array level. By using this innovative 5T+1 configuration, imec’s DTCO study shows a 12.5% smaller bit cell compared to a conventional 6T CFET SRAM cell, with 7-15% faster write operation. This makes the 5T+1 CFET SRAM bit cell an attractive option for prolonging the SRAM scaling roadmap towards A7 and beyond.</p>
<h2>Beyond standard cells: Improved BEOL routability to support the CFET scaling roadmap</h2>
<p>In various DTCO studies, imec has demonstrated the ability to scale CFET device architectures across subsequent logic technology nodes, supported by innovative standard cell configurations and scaling boosters. But as we approach the ångström era, the area advantages at standard cell level can easily be undone by scaling issues in the BEOL, following a new DTCO study presented by imec at 2026 VLSI [6]. In other words: it becomes increasingly difficult to interconnect the various CFET-based standard cells.</p>
<p>Under the ideal scaling scenario where everything scales proportionally, routability stays the same from one node to another. However, starting from the 2nm node, the scaling of some of the ground rules such as the contact poly pitch (CPP, a metric determined by both the gate length and source/drain contact length) and metal-1 pitch has started to slow down. And this increases routing congestion in the wafer frontside, which affects performance, power and area. In addition, aggressive standard cell scaling limits accessibility to the input and output pins.</p>
<h3>Increasing the gear ratio: Improved BEOL routability for CFET-based ångström node technology</h3>
<p>Fortunately, there are several knobs for improving the BEOL routability. One of these is enhancing the so-called gear ratio, which represents the ratio of the CPP to the metal-1 pitch. In 2nm node processor designs, this gear ratio is usually around 1:1. At 2026 VLSI, imec demonstrated through a DTCO study that increasing the gear ratio to 2:1 for A7 CFET-based designs can improve both pin accessibility and area utilization, without compromising power and performance [6]. In practice, this will drive the metal 1 to smaller pitches, requiring more advanced lithography options like single-patterning High NA EUV lithography for its fabrication.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24282408" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig7-BEOL-routing.webp?resize=1352%2C655&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1352" height="655" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig7-BEOL-routing.webp?w=1352&amp;ssl=1 1352w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig7-BEOL-routing.webp?resize=300%2C145&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig7-BEOL-routing.webp?resize=1024%2C496&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig7-BEOL-routing.webp?resize=768%2C372&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/imec_Advancing-CFET-device-roadmap-part2-fig7-BEOL-routing.webp?resize=600%2C291&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 7: Schematic representation of M1 routing for ND2D1 cells in A7 with GR 1:1 and GR 2:1, showing improved pin accessibility for GR 2:1 </strong><strong>(as presented at 2026 VLSI)</strong><strong>.</strong></p>
<h2>Wrapping up Part 2: Enabling the CFET scaling roadmap</h2>
<p>With the double-flip sCFET, imec is introducing a new CFET device architecture into the logic roadmap. Double-flip sCFET has a high scaling potential, offering both split-gate and common-gate device options without area penalty. The novel architecture not only benefits the logic roadmap, but it also provides a solution for the stalled SRAM roadmap by enabling a 5T+1 SRAM CFET bit cell memory. In another DTCO study, imec shows how improved BEOL routability can further support the aggressive scaling of CFET based standard cells.</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Researchers at the <strong>University of California, Santa Cruz</strong> published a technical paper titled “Design Space Exploration of Backside Clock Meshes for 2 nm GAAFET BSPDN Technology.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong> “Clock meshes are used in high-performance VLSI designs to minimize skew and tolerate on-chip variation, but they spend scarce routing resources on premium metal layers. Backside power delivery creates a new option: it adds thick, low-resistance metal layers on the back of the wafer, and the power grid does not consume all of them. Flip-flops remain on the frontside; a backside mesh therefore cannot drive them directly, and every connection passes through a through-silicon via. We present the first design-space exploration of backside clock meshes, implemented in OpenROAD on GT2N, a 2 nm nanosheet technology.&#8221;</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02401">technical paper here.</a> October 2026.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Ali, Wajid, Muhammad Hadir Khan, Dalton Gaddy, and Matthew Guthaus. “Design Space Exploration of Backside Clock Meshes for 2 nm GAAFET BSPDN Technology.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.02401 (October 2026). https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.02401</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">&nbsp;</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Researchers at Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, University of California, Santa Barbara, and National University of Singapore published a technical paper titled “Low contact resistance and high current density in ballistic p-type transistors based on oxygen-doped WSe<sub>2</sub> monolayers.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“The development of high-performance p-type monolayer transistors is critical for extending two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors beyond silicon in sub 1-nm technology nodes for complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) circuits. However, insufficient doping and metal-induced gap states (MIGS) during metal deposition lead to high contact resistance, greatly limiting p-type on-state currents. Here, we demonstrate high-performance ballistic p-type monolayer tungsten diselenide (WSe<sub>2</sub>) transistors by oxygen p-doping. ”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph"><a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-78157-w">Find the technical paper here</a>. October 2026.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Sun, L., Gao, T., Xu, L. et al. Low contact resistance and high current density in ballistic p-type transistors based on oxygen-doped WSe2 monolayers. Nat Commun (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78157-w</p>
